title: Severianus on 2 Corinthians 2
english: God: the matter of deciding through God to come about is not a light thing. Having decided to come to you, I promised this to you not by rashness or lightness; for not according to the flesh do I decide, but spiritually. It is proper that one deciding concerning spiritual things should nowhere be false, so that his yes may be yes and his no, no.

Indeed, whether it is to come or not to come is not in me, but the setting forth in me (2 Kor 1:18). If, therefore, the proclamation had yes and no, my decision regarding my arrival to you would justly have yes and no; but if the word is true, then the whole decision is true. I believe to God that none of those things which we preached is a lie (2 Kor 1:19). For even the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, did not become a liar (2 Kor 1:19). Through Christ we send up the amen to God the Father, and the confirmation toward Christ we received through God; and through the one having sealed us, He demonstrated our belonging to God and our separation from the evil one (2 Kor 1:20–22). For even shepherds place their own seal upon the flocks, distinguishing them from the strangers. Having said 'earnest', He presented that we have received a small deposit of the knowledge, but the perfection is owed to us; for the earnest is a part of the whole.

Because there were many complaints against them, he did not want, having gone, to condemn them (2 Kor 1:23–24). The word is spoken incompletely; for he wants to say that I desired to come to you, but not as one who is lord and teacher of your faith. To stumble you among you, and to correct those stumbling among us, so that we might become fellow-workers of the joy according to God. To believe in you, and in us the correcting of those stumbling, so that we might become fellow-workers of the grace of God. And he says 'joy according to God'; for the apostle would not have joined in with them for a worldly joy. Having spoken of faith, he presented that they are left without works. Therefore, since they have faith as unfruitful and still incomplete, he says he is a fellow-worker to them.

Because of this I did not come, not so that I might not grieve you but myself, and so that I might not condemn anyone on account of what they are doing (2 Kor 2:1). You do not grieve me from those who are alike, and I you; for you grieve me from those from whom you sin, but I grieve you from those whom I strike (2 Kor 2:2). But rejoice...

He appears to be feeling sorrow—for he who has not been grieved clearly shows that he did not even take heed when rebuked (2 Kor 2:3). For even if I grieve you, I am doing a proper thing; cooperate toward my joy regarding your own benefit.

I wrote this, that sparing you, I did not come, so that at the end of this letter, where it lies, lest having come, God might humble me (2 Kor 2:4). And because of this I wrote, so that in gladness I might find you having been corrected, so that you might not grieve. Not looking to my own, but to yours I said this; for I know that if you see me rejoicing, you rejoice, and if you see me grieving, you grieve. I wrote these things so that if you wish for me to come to you, you might beforehand correct the faults.

Showing that he makes the same faults his own, he brought grief and tears, which he has love toward them (2 Kor 2:5). Having said, I wrote to you, not that you might simply be grieved, but that the joy according to God might take away the grief.

If anyone has grieved even him whom you love, he has not grieved me alone, but in part also you, so that I might not burden [you] by saying even Christ (2 Kor 2:6). And he fell silent from saying 'and Christ,' so that he might not burden [you] even by saying it.

He says 'reproof' is the condemnation from the many (2 Kor 2:7). To forgive him this (2 Kor 2:8). Obey me in condemning, obey me also in recalling him who has been condemned (2 Kor 2:9). Forgive him this, he says; for you know that of those which you forgive to this [man], I also desire to forgive (2 Kor 2:10). And because of this he shows that he wants them to think the same things about themselves by a disposition toward them.

He appears to have been grieved toward those in Troas, because they did not do much regarding Titus, nor did they hold him until his arrival, but as if they had become lawless concerning the faith, they departed (2 Kor 2:12-13). Thus, admonishing them as unworthy, he departed even though a door had been opened and no one was closing against the proclamation. Or indeed because of this he departed, as being able easily to correct the things there later upon arrival, as no one being there to hinder.

This is to the one proclaiming our insults and the circumstances through Christ (2 Kor 2:14). But he confesses a greater grace regarding those things through which he is made worthy to triumph through Christ. And he says these things also because of the Corinthians; for it was feared lest they might perhaps slay [him] because of the things...

title: The Law as Ministry of Death vs the Spirit as Ministry of Life
english: Enduring afflictions and falling away from salvation (2 Cor 2:15–16). The idolaters, being in death to the intelligible due to the ignorance and hardness existing in them, fall a second time into death because they do not receive the evangelical preaching; but those who, having come to the beginnings of the knowledge of God through the legal instruction, have perhaps become somewhat in life, yet if they believe in Christ, they receive the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father from life unto life.

Shortly after, he interprets this passage differently. Such things are established by Christ being a fragrance, not of those happening by chance but of those serving God sincerely. And as he does not say these things about himself as a burden, but from which he proceeds, he says, 'for we are not as many as many are,' and he demonstrated himself (2 Cor 2:17).

He says that to peddle the word means to mingle with circumcision and keep Sabbaths, or to think that some consider piety to be a profit. I say, however, that he speaks from sincerity, and says that this very thing is from God, and not from a private power. He also says another thought, that because of this it is from sincerity, since we speak from God, not playing with things but preaching the revelation of God. He says this because there were also false apostles who considered the word concerning piety to be a profit. Then he proceeds from sincerity, instead of 'we do not play with things,' he says, 'but we preach the revelation from God, not peddling the word of God.' The word of God is peddled by mingling with circumcision and the Sabbath and in thinking that piety is a profit.

From here he wants to show how much the law of grace leaves behind, so that none of those from the circumcision, while hypocritically facing those from the Gentiles, might lead them into the observance of the requirement of Moses and the prophets (2 Cor 3:1). This is your faith and your life, becoming a letter to all and a recognition of our preaching (2 Cor 3:2–3). Because of saying 'stony tablets' and 'fleshy hearts,' he shows the superiority of grace over the law, in that the tablet of the soulless heart is greater. He also shows how much the grace of the Spirit remains superior to the law and the ministry of the prophets' preaching.

Higher than the apostles, from themselves rather than from one another (2 Cor 3:5). The letter says the law, but the Spirit says grace (2 Cor 3:6); for the law, while commanding, does not help, but is heavy and kills through punishment those unable to fulfill it, whereas the Spirit makes one clean from sin and provides gifts, clearly leading toward life (2 Cor 3:6). And indeed the glory did not come on tablets but on the face of Moses, as he himself says (2 Cor 3:7–9), because of the glory of his face which was fading (2 Cor 3:7–9).

But not wishing to speak against the prophet Moses, he calls the law Moses, and in this way makes the statement, showing the grace given to Moses to be lesser than the apostolic grace. If he calls the ministry of death—Moses calls it a ministry of death, calling the law death, because it brought forth death through disobedience—yet the law is not slandered by this; for even the apostles are called a stench of death unto death. He calls the apostles a ministry of the Spirit, and Moses a ministry of death. But sparing Moses, he remembers the tablets; Moses brought down tablets from the mountain, but the apostles, having been sent with the Spirit, brought it to the world.

And indeed the glory did not come on tablets but on the face of Moses. And wishing to speak here also regarding Moses, he makes Moses evident through the law. He calls the law itself a minister of death, because the law kills those not fulfilling it. And he does not say this as slandering him, for he also said the apostles are a stench of death because of those not obeying the proclamation. The stench of death is the threat of Gehenna bringing eternal death upon the unbelievers, and the stench of life is the proclamation of the kingdom sending those following the teaching into eternal life. The stench is a forerunner of the reality.

He calls Moses a minister of condemnation and death—for he condemned in the law those not obeying—and the apostles a minister of the Spirit; for Moses brought down the law, but the apostles conveyed the Spirit to the world. The letter of the law, which was glorified, has not been glorified when examined against the surpassing glory of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:10). No one could say that it was glorified in this word.

title: Transformation from Law to Spirit
english: Concerning the comparison with the superior one. 2 Cor 3:11 showed that it was necessary to cease and to be idle regarding the law, but the grace of the Spirit, having been opposed to the law, remains. 2 Cor 3:12–14 Having therefore such a hope. The hope that is seen is not a hope; but he showed that the grace remains, even after the resurrection, receiving the additions, toward the inability of the sons of Israel to gaze intently until the end of the one being made void; for just as they were not able to attend to the glory... so they were not able even to the end of the law, that is, that the law shall be ceased. He says immediately: until today they have a veil. The end of the law is when the veil is taken away and they behold the glory of the Spirit, because in Christ it is made void, that is, it is through the faith into him.

What kind of hope? That the grace of the Spirit is not made void like the law, but remains even after the resurrection. We, because of the blessed hope of the grace of the Spirit remaining, teach with boldness, and we do not imitate the commands of Moses, who through the veil upon the face signaled that the Jews are not able to gaze intently and realize that the law shall receive an end and shall be idle. The veil remains showing no appearance, that the law is made void upon the coming of Christ. 2 Cor 3:15–16 Just as Moses, while speaking to the Jews, had the veil, but returning to the Lord it is taken away, and now the Jews, after reading the law and returning the book, carry the veil as if Moses had returned to the Lord. If therefore, having turned away, you come to the Spirit, your veil is taken away just as Moses' was being taken away when returning to the Lord. 2 Cor 3:17 The one made worthy of the Spirit of the Lord, this one was freed from the condemnation of the law; for through the Spirit the gifts are being worked. And the gift is toward the worthy ones. 2 Cor 3:18 We, he says, the apostles, are seen by men with an unveiled face; but having said this, we all demonstrate the common benefit of the Spirit. And for Moses the glory was not approaching the Israelites, but for us the glory of God is approaching; for having established ourselves on faith, we reflect the glory of God, that is, we see and are being changed as into...

We are being transformed from legal knowledge into spiritual grace, moving from the glory of the Spirit working in us toward the glory of adoption. This is made clear by the Lord Spirit, not the Son of God. Just as one sees in that mirror, and another receives the reflection of the one seeing, so it is with the Spirit; for those reflecting the glory of Christ carry a certain likeness from that glory into glory, that is, they receive and take upon themselves the glory of the spiritual image.

We are being transformed from legal knowledge into spiritual grace, and from the glory not of the law but of the Spirit, into the glory of adoption; for we come to adoption through a washing. He says 'of grace', not 'of the law'; for through the abundance of grace we endure tribulations. The shameful and the base things are hidden, which those practicing strive to hide because of shame; for the base things do not partake of boldness, but wander in darkness. Even if the gospel is covered, it is covered to the unbelieving, not as the glory of Moses' face was covered from all Israel in the law (2 Cor 4:3).

If the god of this age is said to be associated with reading, it follows that he blinded them. But if God blinded, it was supernaturally, as God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see, and 'I hardened the heart of Pharaoh' (Exodus 10:27) according to the spoken word. Just as it was said of a ruler, not that he is naturally a ruler, but that those deceived showed him to be their ruler by obeying him, so also the god of this age has been forbidden, not as being truly God, but because of what the nations say and think, being called God, just as the belly is called the god of gluttons.
